questions.question: Per the lesson “Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets”, a loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st record. Which meter fired, and what does the other meter show?
options: The DML row meter at 10,000 rows, with the statement meter already at its ceiling.
The DML statement meter at 150, while the row meter has barely moved, because one update on a collected list costs a single statement.
The SOQL statement meter at 100, because every update implies a query.
The query row meter at 50,000 rows, which no amount of batching can change.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent counters, and batching the same work into one DML call buys statement headroom, which is the scarce resource in a synchronous save.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Bulkification & Trigger Frameworks: Limits-Aware Design That Scales”, a Bulk API load of 1,000 records hits an object whose trigger is already written for collections. How many times does the trigger execute, and why is each execution safe?
options: Once, because a single DML statement is one transaction with one governor budget.
Five times, because triggers batch at 200 records and each firing is a fresh transaction with its own governor budget.
Two hundred times, once per record, with the budget resetting on every firing.
Once per record, but all the firings share one governor budget.
questions.explanation: Triggers operate on batches of 200 records, so 1,000 records fire the trigger five times, and the design target is the spend inside one firing, not the spend across the load.

A method used with @wire must be cacheable in order to compile, and a cacheable method may perform DML as long as its result is cached.
questions.explanation: LDS and the wire adapters sit on UI API, which returns data and metadata matching the org’s layout and enforces object permissions, FLS, and sharing for the running user.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Security Review: OWASP for Apex, SOQL Injection, and Enforcing CRUD and FLS”, a class declares with sharing and builds dynamic SOQL by concatenating a user-supplied field name and a user-supplied WHERE value. What does with sharing actually do here?
options: It enforces record-level sharing only, so it neither stops the field name injection nor enforces CRUD and FLS.
It blocks both injections, because sharing prevents a user from querying fields their profile hides.
It forces the class to use WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, which the platform adds to the query automatically.
It enforces CRUD and FLS but leaves record visibility to the org-wide default.
questions.explanation: Object permissions, field-level security, and sharing are three separate layers, and the sharing keyword only ever enforces the third one.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The rule that an incident on a lapsed policy is not covered should live in the coverage agent’s prompt, because a model can reason about policy language.
The rule requires policy status, coverage dates, and the incident date to be read together, so it belongs in the aggregate with the policy as root and is checked only through the root.
The rule should be split across the triage and coverage tools so each one enforces the part it can see.
The rule should be enforced by the output schema, which is what typed contracts exist for.
questions.explanation: An aggregate is a consistency boundary, so anything that must stay true together is decided in one place behind the aggregate root rather than combined in free text by the agent.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Asynchronous Apex: Batch, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future, and How to Choose”, a nightly process must reconcile 40,000 Accounts against an ERP, retry failures on the next night’s run, and report a total. Which primitive and pattern fit?
options: A single @Future(callout=true) method that iterates all 40,000 accounts, because future methods run in their own transaction with a larger budget.
Batch Apex with a Database.Stateful counter and a status flag on each record so failed ones are picked up next run, kicked off by a schedulable.
One queueable job per account, enqueued in a loop, so each record’s retry is isolated in its own transaction.
A scheduled class whose execute method performs the reconciliation and the callouts directly, since scheduled Apex is asynchronous.
questions.explanation: Batch Apex is the primitive for volume and gives chunk-level fault isolation, a stateful counter carries the total across chunks, and the scheduler exists only to start it.

A Partial Copy sandbox is where load and performance testing of an integration path belongs.
Performance and load testing of an integration path belongs only in a Full sandbox, while a Partial Copy sandbox with a template is for integration tests that need realistic data.
questions.explanation: Full is the only replica that supports performance and load testing, and Partial Copy with a sandbox template is how you get realistic data into data-dependent integration tests.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Sharing Architecture Deep Dive: Recalculation, Implicit Sharing, and When Sharing Can't Do the Job”, an architect changes a high-volume object’s org-wide default from Private to Read Only on a large org. What runs in the background?
options: Nothing; the flag flips and existing share records are left exactly as they were.
A one-time Apex managed sharing recalculation class, which the architect has to write and associate with the object.
A sharing recalculation that walks existing records and updates share records, and it may also delete shares that now grant no additional access.
A role hierarchy rebuild, because roles determine the default access level for an object.
questions.explanation: A recalculation is a cleanup pass as well as an expansion, so on a large object it is a scheduled event with a maintenance window rather than an impulse change.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: After an imperative write, the wired reads on the same screen need refreshApex, because the cache and the write otherwise disagree and the screen keeps showing stale data.
A write should be wired with cacheable=true so the framework re-provisions the record automatically once it changes.
Data flows from child to parent through @api attributes, and consequences flow back down through events.
Lightning Data Service is a server-side cache, so a component that changes a record leaves every other component on the page unaware.
questions.explanation: Writes are inherently imperative because cacheable methods cannot mutate data, so a wired read on the same screen has to be refreshed explicitly after the write resolves.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Full service, domain, and selector stacks should be applied to every org, including small data-centric apps that could be delivered declaratively.
When a requirement changes, a correctly layered solution touches one class, because every SOQL statement lives in the selector, every object rule in the domain, and every process in the service.
A service method should contain the query, the calculation, and the DML inline so a reviewer can read the whole process in one place.
Triggers are the right home for nontrivial logic because they cannot inherit, which keeps the logic close to the record change.
questions.explanation: Separation of concerns is the payoff: the service orchestrates, the domain owns behavior, and the selector owns queries, so a changed rule or a changed schema touches exactly one class.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?

An object should use a Flow for some rules and a trigger for others, so each mechanism does what it is best at.
Medium density is a hybrid: keep the Record-Triggered Flow as the orchestration layer and move the Map-based, bulk-safe compute into invocable Apex that the Flow calls.
Medium density means migrating straight to Apex, because a Flow plus Apex hybrid creates two entry points on the object.
questions.explanation: The hybrid keeps one readable, ordered entry point in Flow while the pieces Flow cannot express well, such as keyed computes and bulk-safe collection handling, move behind an invocable Apex seam.

The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced at the physical layer too: all platform data, metadata, and pivot tables are partitioned by OrgID using native database partitioning.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Flow Architecture: Flow vs Apex vs External Automation, Decision Framework”, a custom object carries 8,000-record Bulk API loads, fires 40 automations on save, and its updates cascade five levels deep with a real recursion risk. Which architectural standard fits?
options: An Apex trigger behind a metadata framework, because bulk handling and recursion control have to be explicit at high density.
A Record-Triggered Flow, because Flow bulkifies and retries automatically and therefore needs no recursion control.
One large flow with entry conditions on every branch, because a single flow is easier to govern than several.
Both a Record-Triggered Flow and an Apex trigger, one per concern, so each mechanism carries half the load.
questions.explanation: Automation density is measured by automation count, data volume, and dependency sprawl, and only Apex gives a developer explicit control over bulk handling and recursion on a dense object.

A bind variable cannot protect a field or object name, because a name is syntax rather than a value, so user-supplied names must be compared against an allowlist.
questions.explanation: Bind variables and queryWithBinds close value injection, an allowlist closes name injection, escaping is a narrow fallback for quoted literals, and typecasting closes the numeric case.
